t: The Etruscans of central Italy built independent city-states such as Veii, Tarquinia, Caere and Vulci, rich from metals, farming and trade with Greeks and Phoenicians from the 8th century BCE.
They spoke a language unrelated to Latin or Greek, wrote it in an alphabet taken from the Greeks, and are known above all from their tombs, with wall paintings, sculpture and rich grave goods.
By Roman tradition Etruscan kings ruled Rome in the 6th century BCE; from the capture of Veii in 396 BCE Rome conquered Etruria city by city and absorbed its people in the 1st century BCE.
dyk: The longest known Etruscan text, probably a ritual calendar, written on a linen book, survives only because the cloth was cut into strips to wrap an Egyptian mummy, now in the Archaeological Museum in Zagreb.
ev: The Villanovan culture of the early Iron Age appears on the sites of the later Etruscan cities
The first Etruscan inscriptions are written in an alphabet adapted from the Greek
By Roman tradition, Etruscan kings rule Rome, from Tarquinius Priscus to Tarquinius Superbus
Etruscan and Carthaginian ships fight the Phocaean Greeks off Alalia in Corsica
Hiero I of Syracuse destroys an Etruscan fleet off Cumae
Rome captures Veii after a long siege
Rome sacks Volsinii and moves its people to a new site
After the outbreak of the Social War the Etruscans receive Roman citizenship

f.homeland: Etruria, between the Arno and the Tiber in central Italy (Tuscany, northern Lazio and western Umbria), with later cities in the Po valley and in Campania
f.period: c. 900 BCE – 1st century BCE; the Villanovan culture from c. 900 BCE, the height of the city-states in the 7th–5th centuries BCE, conquest by Rome in the 4th–3rd centuries BCE and absorption into Roman Italy by the time of Augustus
f.known: Painted tombs at Tarquinia and the tomb cities of Cerveteri; terracottas and bronzes such as the Apollo of Veii and the Chimera of Arezzo; a non-Indo-European language; divination by haruspices; their influence on early Rome
f.sources: Excavated cities, sanctuaries and above all cemeteries; some 13,000 inscriptions in Etruscan, most of them short, among them the Pyrgi Tablets and the Liber Linteus; Greek and Roman writers such as Herodotus, Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus
